summary: A war between coalitions of kings leads to the capture of Lot and other people and goods from Sodom. Abram leads trained men from his household to pursue and recover the captives; Melchizedek blesses Abram, while Abram refuses the king of Sodom’s offer of goods for himself and protects his allies’ share.
whyItMatters: The chapter shows Abram acting for a relative amid regional violence, then deciding whom to credit for the victory and whose gifts to accept. The women and other captives recovered alongside Lot should remain visible.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: The valley of Siddim, Abram’s camp by Mamre, the pursuit northward, and the return meeting.
context.literaryForm: War report and rescue narrative followed by two contrasting encounters over blessing and recovered goods.

before.text: Lot has moved toward Sodom after separating from Abram, and the narrator has called the city’s people wicked.

here.text: Regional war captures Lot and others; track Abram’s rescue and the distinct responses of Melchizedek and Sodom’s king.

after.text: After the conflict, Yahweh speaks to Abram in a vision about protection, an heir, and the future of his descendants.

outline.heading: Kings, tribute, and rebellion
outline.note: Four kings and five kings are named, and a vassal revolt begins the war.

outline.heading: Campaign and battle
outline.note: The invading coalition strikes groups across the region and defeats the kings near tar pits.

outline.heading: Captives taken; Abram pursues
outline.note: Goods, food, Lot, and others are carried off; Abram and allies recover them.

outline.heading: Melchizedek’s blessing
outline.note: The priest-king brings bread and wine, blesses Abram, and receives a tenth.

outline.heading: Abram refuses Sodom’s goods
outline.note: Abram rejects personal gain from Sodom while allowing provisions and allies’ portions.

keyVerses.text: They took Lot, Abram’s brother’s son, who lived in Sodom, and his goods, and departed.
keyVerses.why: Lot’s captivity connects the earlier choice of Sodom to Abram’s rescue.

keyVerses.text: He brought back all the goods, and also brought back his relative Lot and his goods, and the women also, and the other people.
keyVerses.why: The recovery includes women and other people, not only a wealthy relative.

keyVerses.text: Blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.” Abram gave him a tenth of all.
keyVerses.why: The blessing credits God Most High with the victory before Abram gives a tenth.

questions.question: Why is Lot caught up in the war?
questions.answer: Lot lives in Sodom when the city and its neighbors lose to the invading kings. The victors take goods and food and also carry him off, linking his earlier move to this danger.

questions.question: What are the tar pits doing in the battle scene?
questions.answer: The valley of Siddim is described as full of them, and some fleeing kings fall there. The detail helps explain the battlefield’s danger without requiring a precise modern reconstruction of the war.

questions.question: Does Abram rescue only Lot?
questions.answer: No. The return includes all recovered goods, Lot and his goods, women, and other people. A retelling focused only on the male relative would erase the wider group taken in the raid.

questions.question: How does Abram organize the rescue?
questions.answer: After hearing of Lot’s capture, Abram leads 318 trained men born in his household, pursues the raiders, and divides his force for a night attack. The chapter also names regional allies.

questions.question: Who is Melchizedek in this chapter?
questions.answer: He is called king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He brings bread and wine, blesses Abram, and says God delivered the enemies into Abram’s hand; the chapter gives no further biography.

questions.question: What does Abram’s tenth signify in this scene?
questions.answer: After Melchizedek blesses him and credits God Most High for the victory, Abram gives him a tenth of all. The episode records a gift here but does not spell out a later universal tax or worship rule.

questions.question: Why refuse the king of Sodom’s reward while letting allies take shares?
questions.answer: Abram says he has sworn not to take even a thread for himself, lest the king claim to have made him rich. He distinguishes his own refusal from food already consumed and the portions due to Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre.

questions.question: Is the victory portrayed as Abram’s strength alone?
questions.answer: The account describes a planned pursuit by Abram and his men, while Melchizedek’s blessing credits God Most High with handing over the enemies. The text holds human action and divine thanks together in the return scene.

glossary.def: The battle valley, identified in the chapter with the Salt Sea and described as containing tar pits.
The king of Salem and priest of God Most High who blesses Abram after the rescue.
The portion Abram gives Melchizedek after the blessing.
